Excerpts from the dissertation on images

b.bio: Noël Alexandre (Natalis Alexander), born at Rouen on 19 January 1639, entered the Dominicans there in 1655 (9 May) and afterwards studied and taught philosophy, theology, and ecclesiastical law for twelve years at Saint-Jacques in Paris, taking his Sorbonne doctorate in 1675. His Selecta historiae ecclesiasticae capita (24 vols., 1676–86) made him a leading ecclesiastical historian. He defended Gallican positions and Jansenist sympathies against Rome: he was banished to Châtellerault in 1709 for subscribing to the Jansenist Cas de conscience (1703) and lost his pension in 1713. He died in Paris on 21 August 1724.
b.s: The works held here are from the historical-dissertation apparatus of his Selecta historiae ecclesiasticae capita: a dissertation on sacred images which surveys authorities and argues that worship of any but God is idolatrous error, that relics may be honored but images never adored, and that only latria (not veneration) is forbidden to images — opposing Robert Bellarmine and the Carolingian opposition to Nicaea II (Frankfurt's condemnation of the seventh synod); and a historical notice on Sylvester II.

w: To a Foreigner Who Loves Spanish Affairs

b.bio: Nicolás Antonio was born in Seville on 31 July 1617 and took his degree at Salamanca (1636–1639). Philip IV conferred the Order of Santiago on him in 1645 and sent him to Rome as General Agent in 1654; he returned to Spain in 1679 and died at Madrid in the spring of 1684. He is remembered as a bibliographer: his Bibliotheca Hispana nova appeared at Rome in 1672 under the title Bibliotheca Hispana sive Hispanorum, and the Bibliotheca Hispana vetus, a literary history of Spain from Augustus to the end of the fifteenth century, was published posthumously at Rome in 1696 under Cardinal José Sáenz de Aguirre. His Censura de historias fabulosas, printed at Valencia in 1742, combined erudition with critical judgment on legendary histories.
b.s: The works held here are his short historical and critical notices — chiefly sorting out the identity and career of Julian of Toledo (distinguishing monk-Julian from bishop-Julian, dating his succession to Quiricus in 681, and defending the authenticity of his Eucharistic apologetics, addressed to Benedict II rather than Leo II, against Baronius and others), which show the critical method behind the Bibliotheca Hispana.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author. They cover Nicolas Charmot (c. 1655–1714), a French missionary priest in China and procurator in Rome who wrote on the Chinese rites controversy, and Sébastien-Roch Nicolas Chamfort (1741–1794), the revolutionary-era writer of epigrams; neither matches a Latin patristic or medieval author represented by a single-page dedication letter in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 203). The library's single page is a dedication letter arguing that holiness rather than office makes an heir to the saint, addressed against rebels and citing Bernard.
b.s: The work held here is a one-page dedicatory letter asserting that virtue and piety, not rank or office, make one worthy of a saint's inheritance.

w: Notice on the Book on the Deaths of the Persecutors

b.bio: Nicolas Lenglet Du Fresnoy was a French polygraph born on 5 October 1674 (Paris according to the Dictionnaire Port-Royal; some accounts give Beauvais) and died in Paris on 16 January 1755. He studied theology at the Sorbonne as 'domestique' of Edme Pirot and frequented Bossuet's circle, but his first book — an ironic attack on Maria d'Agreda's Mystical City of God — provoked his arrest by La Reynie, a short stay in the Bastille, and exclusion from the Sorbonne house. In 1705 Torcy appointed him secretary for Latin and French languages to the Elector of Cologne, who resided at Lille; he returned to Paris during the Regency and made editing, bibliography, geography, and clandestine publishing his trade. His opposition to royal censors brought repeated imprisonments (five periods in the Bastille, plus the Strasbourg citadel and the Château de Vincennes) under Louis XV.
b.s: The works held here are his editorial apparatus for Lactantius in the Patrologia Latina: a preface arguing that the Divine Institutes answers pagan philosophical attacks and refutes pagan philosophy before teaching Christian truth, dates the work after 315 (c. 320), and reads Book VI against Licinius' apostasy (with the licinian persecution confined to the eastern empire), plus a notice on De Mortibus Persecutorum.

w: Preface to the fragments of Hilary

b.bio: None of The surviving records identifies this Nicolas Faber. They describe instead a fifteenth-century Swiss Dominican pilgrim-writer (Felix Fabri/Faber), a Leipzig Protestant printer (Nicolaus Faber, c. 1490–1554), and a Franciscan controversialist (Nicolaus Ferber, d. 1534) — different men with similar names, none connected to patristic editing, so their biographical details cannot be used here. What is known comes from the library record alone: an author under this name wrote the prefatory essay to the fragments of Hilary of Poitiers printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 10.
b.s: His preface introduces and frames Hilary's fragmentary anti-Arian material, surveying the historical controversy over Ursacius and Valens at Constantius's court and drawing on Athanasius, Jerome, Socrates, Sozomen, Epiphanius, and Augustine to establish the text's context.

b.bio: Nicolas Gervaise was born in Paris around 1662 or 1663, the son of the physician of Fouquet. He left for the Siam mission on 19 January 1681 at about eighteen, studied theology at the Collège général there, learned Siamese, and left the Missions Étrangères in 1685 with two sons of the king of Gowa (Makassar), whom he presented at court. Later he held a charge at Vannes (described variously as curé or rector). He wrote on Siam, Makassar, Saint Martin of Tours, and Boethius. Appointed titular bishop of Horrea and ordained bishop on 11 June 1726 by Pope Benedict XIII, he led a mission to the Orinoco region and was killed with his companions by Galibi (Carib) Indians on 20 November 1729.
b.s: The works held here are his Histoire de Boëce with analyses of all Boethius's writings (PL 64): a life arguing that Boethius was a saint and martyr who converted the Burgundians, plus running analyses treating the Church, Christology, the Trinity, providence, grace, free will, and baptism as they arise from Boethius's texts, arguing against Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians, the predestinarian party, and Dupin.

b.bio: The library holds under this name a single four-page Preface printed in PL 63, the Migne volume containing Boethius's theological opuscula and related sixth-century texts. No source consulted gives dates, birthplace, or office for this Nicolaus Judecus. The name must be kept apart from several better-documented men called Nicolaus whom searches turn up: Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), cardinal and philosopher; Nicolaus de Mirabilibus (d. 1495), Transylvanian Dominican; and Nicolaus van Esch (1507–1578), Dutch Catholic theologian. None of these is the author of the piece held here.
b.s: The work here is a brief prefatory text in PL 63 attached to the Boethius-Ennodius volume; its value to readers lies in its placement among sixth-century Latin patristic materials rather than in any documented career of its author.

w: Dissertation on the Book on the Anger of God
Dissertation on the Book on the Deaths of the Persecutors
Dissertation on the Book which is Inscribed Octavius

b.bio: Denis-Nicolas Le Nourry was born at Dieppe in Normandy on 18 February 1647 and entered the Benedictine Order at Jumièges on 8 July 1665. After ordination he worked at Rouen, assisting Jean Garet on the edition of Cassiodorus (1679) and Jean du Chesne and Julien Bellaise on Ambrose, then aided Jacques Du Frische at Paris, where he spent his last forty years at the Abbey of St-Germain, dying there on 24 March 1724. His principal work is the Apparatus ad bibliothecam maximam veterum patrum et antiquorum scriptorum (Paris, 1703 and 1715), a set of dissertations prefacing the Lyon collection of the Fathers, treating each writer's life, the occasion, design, scope and genuineness of each work, its historical setting, and its struggle against heathenism or heresy. He also edited Cyprian's Liber ad Donatum de mortibus persecutorum (1710). The dissertations held here — on Tertullian's Apologeticum, Minucius Felix's Octavius, Lactantius's Divine Institutes and De ira Dei, and related texts — come from that apparatus.
b.s: His Apparatus supplied standard scholarly introductions to the ante-Nicene apologists, and the dissertations here defend their genuineness and argue their case against paganism, engaging critics such as Rigaltius and Petavius.

w: On the Author of the Book on the Deaths of the Persecutors

b.bio: None of the surviving records describes this author; the bishop Hugues Lestoquer (d. 1408) and Nicholas of Lyra are different persons and are set aside. What is known comes from the library record: under this name the library holds a seven-page dissertation printed among the appendices to Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 7, written against Dom Nicolas Le Nourry, the Benedictine of Saint-Maur whose Apparatus had denied that Lactantius wrote De mortibus persecutorum. Lestoq answers him point by point: corrupt readings are faults of scribes, not the author; Jerome attests the title; the same Donatus dedicated both books; and providence must be defended by reason against the philosophers who deny it.
b.s: His dissertation is a brief but focused contribution to the eighteenth-century debate over whether Lactantius authored De mortibus persecutorum, arguing the affirmative against Dom Le Nourry.

b.bio: Nalgod (Nalgodus) was a monk of Cluny who rewrote an earlier, disorderly Life of Saint Odo of Cluny by one Joannes, prompted by senior monks of the community. He states in his prologue that he writes in a plain domestic style because the saint's deeds were buried under verbal confusion and disordered narration, and that his labor is for the future profit of readers rather than adorned for glory. The Légendiers latins database also credits him with a Vita of Maiolus.
b.s: His Vita S. Odonis is the library's held work: a rewritten hagiography of Odo, first founder/abbot of Cluny, arguing that plain truthful style honors the saint better than eloquence and that returning to God's service is true liberty.

b.bio: Nazarius was a Latin rhetorician and panegyrist, a professor of rhetoric at Bordeaux according to Ausonius. Jerome's Chronicle calls him an eminent rhetor under 315 CE ('Nazarius insignis rhetor habetur'). His one securely attested speech, delivered at Rome in 321 at the beginning of the fifth year of the Caesars Crispus and Constantine, celebrates the fifteenth anniversary of Constantine's accession and praises Constantine as the exemplar of every virtue to his sons. A 313 speech on the victory over Maxentius has often been attributed to him, but differences of style and vocabulary argue against it.
b.s: The work held here is his 321 panegyric to Constantine, a primary witness to how imperial ideology, providence, and civic religion were framed in praise-speech under the first Christian emperor.

b.bio: the surviving records describe a different man of the same name: Nicetas of Remesiana, a late-fourth-century bishop of Remesiana in Dacia and friend of Paulinus of Nola, whose works were catechetical instructions and hymns. That is not the author of the book held here, so those sources cannot be used for this note. The work in this library is a short polemic against the 'azymites' — those who use unleavened bread in the eucharist — directed against the Romans and the Latins, arguing that unleavened bread is not true bread and that the eucharistic bread is made Christ's living body, consubstantial with us. The library record does not identify the author beyond the name 'Niceta', so no dates, see, or offices can be asserted.
b.s: His single short treatise here is a specimen of the case that unleavened bread keeps communicants under the law's shadow, while leavened bread, perfected by leaven, becomes Christ's body consubstantial with us.

b.bio: the surviving records describe Nicolaus Avancini (1611–1686), an Italian Jesuit ascetical writer and playwright of the Tyrol — a different person from a different century, and not the author of the work held here. The library's record is decisive: under the name Nicolaus Avagonius it holds a two-page historical text in PL 179 concerning the schism of Peter of Pierleone (Antipope Anacletus II). Nothing in the sources gives dates or offices for this Avagonius, so none are asserted.
b.s: The fragment here is a brief pro-papal account of the Anacletan schism, arguing that metropolitan primacy and imperial legitimacy flow from papal grant and that armed force may restore the true pope.

b.bio: The library prints this author as Nicholas of Cluny, but the sources identify him as Nicholas of Clairvaux (also Nicholas of Montiéramey), a French monk who entered Benedictine Montiéramey near Troyes, joined the Cistercians at Clairvaux in 1145–1146, and served as a secretary of Bernard of Clairvaux until Bernard dismissed him in 1151 for misusing the abbot's seals after a visit to Cluny — which may explain the Cluny attribution. He later presented Bernard's sermons to Pope Adrian IV in Rome, entered the service of Count Henry I of Champagne, and became prior of Saint-Jean-in-Châtel in 1160.
b.s: His letters and sermons survive in large part because of his close association with Bernard of Clairvaux; the epistle held here argues that true liberality conforms to all without ambition, citing Cicero.

b.bio: The sources identify a Franciscan preacher and doctor of theology at Lyon, active around the turn of the fourteenth century, with unknown birth and death dates. His attested works are sermon collections — Sermones dominicales and Sermones de sanctis et festis — printed at Paris and Lyon between 1486 and 1519 in editions associated with Jean Quentin, and listed in medieval English library catalogues such as Syon Abbey and Westminster. Those sources do not mention a praise of St. Bernard, so the attribution of the single page held here under his name cannot be confirmed from them.
b.s: He is remembered as a popular late medieval preacher whose exemplum-rich sermons circulated widely in manuscript and print; the work held here, an exhortation on the fleetingness of present life and the joys prepared after death, is attributed to him by the library record alone.

b.bio: Gerard of Burgundy, born at Chevron in Savoy between 990 and 995, was a canon at Liège and became bishop of Florence in 1045 (the Catholic Encyclopedia says 1046), where he restored the canonical life among the clergy. He was elected pope at Siena in December 1058 and reigned from 24 January 1059 until his death at Florence on 27 July 1061 (the Catholic Encyclopedia also records 19 July as a possible date). His election followed the irregular elevation of the antipope Benedict X by the Tusculan party. As pope he extended papal influence in Milan and southern Italy and issued the election decree of 1059 restricting papal elections to the cardinal bishops.
b.s: The letters and diplomas held here concern papal privilege (violation of which incurs anathema), clerical immunity from lay jurisdiction, monastic exemption from diocesan bishops with appeal to the apostolic see protecting monks, free abbatial election confirmed by the Roman pontiff, and marriage forbidden within seven degrees of kinship — documents of the reforming papacy on the eve of the Investiture Controversy.

b.bio: Nicholas of Worcester was an English monk, baptised and taught by Bishop Wulfstan of Worcester and sent by him to study under Lanfranc at Christchurch, Canterbury. He succeeded Thomas as prior of Worcester — sources differ on the year, giving 1113 or c. 1116 — and held the office until his death on 24 June 1124. William of Malmesbury called him of exalted descent; Emma Mason argues he was a son of King Harold Godwinson. He corresponded with Eadmer, John of Worcester, and Malmesbury, who valued his help with their histories.
b.s: The library holds his letter to Eadmer (PL 159), which treats the dispute between the churches of York and Scotland, arguing both that York holds primacy over the Scots and, against York, that York received faith and orders from the Scottish church, that the Scottish church possesses liberty and dignity against York, that consecration should be sought from the apostolic see, and that litigation between churches should be dissolved.

w: Prologue on the commendation of Holy Scripture
Prologue on the intention of the author
Prologue to the moralities of the Bible

b.bio: Nicholas of Lyra was born around 1270 at Lyre in Normandy and entered the Franciscan order at Verneuil-sur-Avre in 1291. He was a doctor at the Sorbonne by 1309 and ten years later was appointed head of all Franciscans in France. Sources differ on his death year: the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1340, while Wikipedia and ULAN give October 1349. His major work, the Postillae perpetuae in universam S. Scripturam, printed at Rome in 1471, was the first printed commentary on the Bible. The report that he was of Jewish descent dates only from the fifteenth century and has been dismissed by some modern scholars.
b.s: Among the most influential medieval Christian exegetes, whose literal-sense method — which he held to be the foundation of all mystical expositions — shaped later readers of Scripture down to Luther; the library holds three of his prologues on Scripture's commendation, the author's intention, and its moralities.

w: On the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious

b.bio: Nithard was a Frankish count, son of Angilbert and of Bertha, daughter of Charlemagne. He was probably raised either at court or at Saint-Riquier, where his father was lay abbot. He served his cousin Charles the Bald as counselor and ambassador to Lothair in 840, and fought at Fontenoy in 841. At Charles's request he wrote the four books held here, narrating the quarrels of Louis the Pious's sons down to 843 in order to establish Charles's right. He probably died of wounds received fighting the Northmen near Angoulême; the date is disputed among scholars, with consensus for June 14, 844.
b.s: The only layman of his time who devoted himself to writing history, he gives an eyewitness, partisan account of the Carolingian civil war that defends Charles the Bald against Lothair.

b.bio: The library prints this name for Norbert of Xanten (also known as Norbert of Magdeburg), who became Archbishop of Magdeburg and died there on 6 June 1134. Born near Xanten on the Rhine around 1080, he served as canon at Xanten and almoner to Emperor Henry V before a conversion led him to itinerant preaching and the founding of the Premonstratensian canons regular at Prémontré. He was canonized by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582. The sources describe his career as reformer and bishop; they do not document authorship of the sermons printed under his name in PL 170, which cite later biographies of him.
b.s: The single work held here is a sermon printed in PL 170 under his name, treating schism as the devil's work against church unity, repentance for crimes against the priesthood, and mission resting on grace rather than merit.

b.bio: Novatus Catholicus is a Latin ecclesiastical writer whom the Wikisource record places in the fifth to sixth century, describing him as a Roman bishop and theologian. He should not be confused with the third-century Roman priest and antipope Novatian, whose name Greek writers rendered as 'Novatus'; the works held here are moral-exegetical pieces on humility and obedience, not the rigorist schismatic writings of the Novatians. Beyond the century range and the title given by that record, no secure dates or career details are attested in the sources consulted.
b.s: The two short moral-exegetical texts preserved under his name argue that true humility seeks God rather than human praise, that obedience to superiors is obedience to God, and that grace together with consent conquers sin.

b.bio: Nicolaus Serarius was born 5 December 1555 at Rambervillers in Lorraine. He entered the Society of Jesus on 3 March 1573 after studying philosophy at Cologne, taught philosophy and then theology at the University of Würzburg (serving as prorector 1589–1590 and taking his doctorate there in 1591), and from 1595 to 1608 was professor of theology, at times of Scripture, at the Jesuit college attached to the University of Mainz. Sources differ on his death: McClintock and Strong give Mainz, 20 May 1610; Germania Sacra, Wikipedia, and the Mainz professors' catalogue give 30 May 1609. His published work was chiefly biblical commentary — on Joshua through the Chronicles — and a five-book history of the archbishops and city of Mainz.
b.s: The library holds only his two-page preface to volume 89 of the Patrologia Latina. His wider reputation rests on his biblical commentaries and his five-book Moguntiacarum Rerum on the archdiocese and city of Mainz, which was later incorporated, with annotations and additions, into Georg Christian Joannis's collection of sources on Mainz history.

w: Notes on the Book on the Deaths of the Persecutors

b.bio: Nicolas Toinard (also Thoynard), born at Orléans (baptized 5 March 1629 at Saint-Pierre-Lentin), died in Paris 5 January 1706, was a French philologist and numismatist. Trained in law (bachelor and licentiate) but drawn to sacred and profane antiquity, he moved to Paris in 1652, befriended the bibliophile Émery Bigot, and attended the scholarly gatherings of Jacques Dupuy, keeper of the Bibliothèque du Roi. He also wrote a dissertation on Commodus's age on coins (1690) and an evangelical harmony published posthumously (1716).
b.s: The works held here are his critical notes on Lactantius's De mortibus persecutorum: textual emendations (including 'post' corrected to 'ante') and chronological arguments on Peter's Roman see and the twenty-one-year interval from the Passion to Nero, argued against Henry Dodwell, Du Cange, Pagius, Baluze, and the Paschal Chronicle.

b.bio: None of The surviving records treats a Nicetas of Maroneia; they describe separate figures of the same name — Nicetas of Nicomedia, a twelfth-century archbishop who debated Anselm of Havelberg in Constantinople in 1136; Nicetas of Remesiana (c. 335–414); Nicetas I of Constantinople (d. 780); and Nicetas of Medikion (d. 824) — none of which can be attached to this author. What the library holds under this name is a single short Greek work in PG 139: a dialogue on the procession of the Holy Spirit, arguing against the Latin Filioque while also pressing the Greek side, treating the Trinity, subsistent relations, divine simplicity, and the claim that the Filioque dispute caused the Greek-Latin schism.
b.s: The work here is a Byzantine anti-Filioque dialogue that stages the Greek-Latin dispute over the Spirit's procession as a formal exchange of objections, responses, and proofs.

b.bio: Nicholas Cabasilas was born in Thessalonica around 1320–1322, nephew of Neilos Cabasilas. He was once thought to have succeeded his uncle as archbishop of Thessalonica in 1355, but contemporary records of that see do not list him; he more likely served as a priest at the Mangana Monastery in Constantinople. He advised Emperor John VI Cantacuzenus during the civil war of 1341–1347, supported Gregory Palamas in the Hesychast controversy, and apparently became a monk at Mangana late in life. He is remembered chiefly for Life in Christ and the Commentary on the Divine Liturgy.
b.s: His two treatises are classics of Eastern sacramental theology, teaching union with Christ through baptism, chrismation, and the Eucharist. Note that the PG 150 pages held here also contain material arguing against Lutheran and Zwinglian eucharistic doctrine (and even against 'Cabasila'), which cannot be from Cabasilas himself and appears to be later editorial matter bound with his works.

b.bio: Tommaso Parentucelli, born at Sarzana in Liguria on 15 November 1397, died in Rome 24 March 1455. Trained at Bologna and Florence as tutor to the Strozzi and Albizzi families, he served Bishop Niccolò Albergati of Bologna for over twenty years, took a master's degree in theology in 1422, was made cardinal by Eugene IV in 1446, and was elected pope on 6 March 1447. His pontificate saw the fall of Constantinople, the submission of antipope Felix V, the Concordat of Vienna, and his founding of the Vatican Library. However, the two 'Addenda' volumes held here under his name sit in PG 160 among Greek patristic texts, cite Leo Allatius (a seventeenth-century scholar), and argue for church union against 'the Greeks' — material that cannot plausibly be his composition.
b.s: The works catalogued under this name are almost certainly misattributed: they are Greek-father addenda defending papal primacy and church union, written after Nicholas V's death, while the historical pope is remembered chiefly for founding the Vatican Library rather than for theological writing.
